findings.title: AttributeError: get_supported_language_variant has no cache_clear (lru_cache removed)
findings.description:
The diff changes `_get_supported_language_variant.cache_clear()` to `get_supported_language_variant.cache_clear()`. However, `get_supported_language_variant` is now a regular function (not decorated with `lru_cache`), so it does not have a `cache_clear` attribute. Calling `get_supported_language_variant.cache_clear()` will raise an `AttributeError` at runtime when `reset_cache` is invoked with `setting` in `("LANGUAGES", "LANGUAGE_CODE")`. This is a critical bug: any call to `reset_cache` will crash.

_LogicAgent:_ The diff removes the `@functools.lru_cache` decorator that was on the private helper `_get_supported_language_variant`, but leaves a stale docstring comment in `get_supported_language_variant` claiming that `lru_cache` should have a maxsize. More importantly, by inlining the logic and removing the cache, the function now performs a fresh lookup on every call. However, the docstring says 'lru_cache should have a maxsize to prevent from memory exhaustion attacks' which is now factually incorrect since there is no lru_cache on this function anymore. This is a documentation inconsistency, not a runtime bug, but it will mislead future developers into thinking there's a cache that can be exhausted when there isn't. The actual security concern (memory exhaustion from unbounded distinct keys in a cache) is mitigated by the length check that now happens before the lookup, but the comment is misleading.
findings.suggestion: Since `get_supported_language_variant` is no longer wrapped with `lru_cache`, remove the `get_supported_language_variant.cache_clear()` call. If caching is still desired, re-introduce `lru_cache` on the function, or replace with a manual cache that exposes a `clear` method.

findings.title: strict=True + long code now always raises LookupError, even if a prefix matches
findings.description: When `strict` is True and `lang_code` is longer than `LANGUAGE_CODE_MAX_LENGTH`, the function raises `LookupError`. This is a behavioral change from the old code. In the old code, `_get_supported_language_variant` was called with the full `lang_code` and could still find a match if the full code happened to be in the supported list (unlikely for very long codes, but theoretically possible). The new code explicitly rejects any `strict` lookup for codes over the max length. This is likely intentional (long codes are suspicious), but it's a logic change: `strict=True` with a very long code that was previously accepted (if it matched a supported language) will now always raise. Given that supported language codes are short, this is unlikely to break real-world cases, but it is a semantic change.
findings.suggestion: Confirm that this is intended: `strict=True` with a very long code should always raise `LookupError` regardless of whether a prefix might match. If so, add a comment noting this intentional behavior. If not, reconsider whether the length check should apply before the `strict` check in the strict case.

findings.title: Subtle use of i=None as rfind bound
findings.description: The variable `i` is initialized to `None`, and the walrus operator `i := lang_code.rfind("-", 0, i)` is used. On the first call, `i` is `None`, so `rfind` receives `None` as the `end` parameter. Python's `str.rfind` treats `None` as the end of the string, which is correct. On subsequent calls, `i` is an integer, which is also correct. However, this is a subtle pattern: the initial value of `i` being `None` is only safe because `rfind` accepts `None`. If this code were ported to a language or context where `None`/`null` is not a valid bound, it would fail. In Python, this works, but it's a fragile pattern. More importantly, the loop will terminate because `rfind` returns -1 when the substring is not found, and the condition is `> -1`. This is correct.
findings.suggestion: This is fine in Python, but consider adding a brief comment that `i=None` is valid for `rfind` (meaning 'search to end of string') to prevent confusion for future maintainers.

findings.title: Potential O(n) membership test in supported_lang_codes
findings.description: The expression `code.lower() in supported_lang_codes` performs a case-insensitive lookup, but `supported_lang_codes` is a list (or set) of language codes returned by `get_languages()`. If `get_languages()` returns codes in mixed case, the `.lower()` comparison may not match. The original code had the same logic, so this is not a regression. However, `in` on a list is O(n), and `supported_lang_codes` could be large. If `get_languages()` returns a list, this is a performance concern. If it returns a set, it's fine. The original code had the same issue, so this is not a new bug, but worth noting.
findings.suggestion: Verify that `get_languages()` returns a set or that the list is small enough that O(n) lookup is acceptable. If it returns a list, consider converting to a set for faster membership testing.
